question: A patient with cryptococcal meningitis is started on conventional amphotericin B deoxycholate. Which statement best explains both its antifungal mechanism and its dose-limiting toxicity?

answers.text: AmB binds ergosterol in the fungal membrane, forming pores that cause ion leakage and cell death; it also binds cholesterol in human renal tubular cells, causing nephrotoxicity.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. AmB's polyene macrolide ring has high affinity for ergosterol (10× > cholesterol) but does also bind cholesterol — this explains its nephrotoxicity (tubular damage, renal tubular acidosis, hypokalaemia). Lipid formulations (L-AmB) reduce nephrotoxicity by altering tissue distribution.

answers.text: AmB inhibits ergosterol synthesis by blocking lanosterol 14α-demethylase; renal toxicity arises from crystalluria.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Lanosterol 14α-demethylase inhibition is the mechanism of azoles (e.g., fluconazole), not amphotericin B. AmB binds ergosterol directly rather than inhibiting its synthesis.

answers.text: AmB inhibits β-1,3-glucan synthase in the fungal cell wall; toxicity is primarily hepatotoxicity.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: β-1,3-glucan synthase inhibition is the mechanism of echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin), not amphotericin B.

answers.text: AmB acts as a fungistatic agent that allows the immune system to clear Cryptococcus; toxicity is primarily bone marrow suppression.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: AmB is fungicidal, not merely fungistatic, against Cryptococcus. Its primary toxicity is nephrotoxicity (and infusion reactions), not bone marrow suppression.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the Polyenes and Azoles block. AmB binds ergosterol (mechanism) and also binds cholesterol in human renal cells (toxicity mechanism).
Well done. AmB's dual ergosterol/cholesterol binding explains both its broad-spectrum efficacy and its renal toxicity — the key trade-off managed with lipid formulations.
